fields.result: Output probability in channel 2 becomes completely energy-independent ($P_2 = 1/2$ for equal-weight normalized input) when coupling parameters and input amplitudes satisfy $J_2 = 2J_1$ and $\alpha_1 = -\alpha_2$.
fields.question: How do coupling asymmetry, atom-cavity detuning, and coherent multichannel input state preparation jointly determine single-photon routing in a Jaynes-Cummings cavity-waveguide network?
fields.limits: Single-excitation subspace; linear waveguide dispersion; no direct interwaveguide coupling; point-like cavity-waveguide delta couplings.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4 : (Color online) Output probabilities $P_{1}$ , $P_{2}$ , and $P_{3}$ as functions of the normalized photon energy $\varepsilon/\omega_{0}$ for a single photon prepared in a coherent superposition of input channels 1 and 2 with amplitudes $\alpha_{1}$ and $\alpha_{2}$ . The plotted values for relative input amplitudes ( $a_{1},a_{2}$ )= (1, 0), (0.75, 0.25), (1, -1), and (0.5, 0.5) for asymmetric couplings $J_{1}=0.005\omega_{0}$ and $J_{2}=0.01\omega_{0}$ in the lossless limit.

fields.result: Introduced differentiable-digital-twin software framework `qruise-toolset` for atomic qubits, simulating single-qubit randomized benchmarking with error per Clifford of $1.11(30)\times 10^{-3}$ and achieving quantum volume of $2^{4}=16$ with $83.1\%$ mean heavy-output probability.
fields.question: How can atomic quantum processor dynamics and hardware control stacks be modelled and calibrated using end-to-end automatic differentiation?
fields.limits: Demonstrated primarily in numerical simulation; subject to exponential resource scaling for full state and process tomography.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 18 : Quantum-volume benchmark of the simulated four-qubit Rydberg-atom register. Each marker is the heavy-output probability (HOP) of one random square circuit of width and depth four, evaluated from 200 shots per circuit; heavy outputs are the ideal bit strings whose simulated probabilities exceed the median. The solid line is the cumulative mean HOP over the 200 circuits, and the dashed line marks the $2/3$ pass threshold. The mean HOP reaches $83.1\%$ , above the threshold, so the processor passes at dimension $d=4$ , corresponding to a quantum volume of $2^{4}=16$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Heavy-output probability per circuit for 200 random four-qubit square circuits of depth 4. The cumulative mean (solid line) stays at $83.1\%$, exceeding the $2/3$ pass threshold (dashed line) to demonstrate a quantum volume of 16.

fields.result: Simulated parametric-resonance $\mathrm{CZ}$ gates across three pairs of fixed-frequency transmon qubits sharing one tunable coupler achieve target-subspace fidelities of 0.9943 ($\mathrm{CZ}_{01}$), 0.9834 ($\mathrm{CZ}_{02}$), and 0.9907 ($\mathrm{CZ}_{12}$). A spectator qubit initially in state $|1\rangle$ suffers significant population distortion, transferring population or leaving the computational space.
fields.question: Can selective parametric-resonance $\mathrm{CZ}$ gates be implemented between all pairs of fixed-frequency transmon qubits connected to a single tunable coupler using only coupler flux modulation?
fields.limits: Numerical simulation only, with three energy levels per component and no decoherence, relaxation, dephasing, or flux noise modeled; target fidelities evaluated only on the four-state subspace where the spectator qubit and coupler remain in $|0\rangle$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: State populations under the flux applied to the coupler. The populations of $|0110\rangle$ , $|0020\rangle$ , and $|0200\rangle$ are shown over $500\;ns$ . The rise and fall times are both 50 $ns$ , as indicated by the gray regions. An interaction is observed with $|0020\rangle$ , whereas no appreciable interaction occurs with $|0200\rangle$ . This illustrates the importance of selecting the bare state and the dressed state that mediates its interaction when implementing a $\mathrm{CZ}$ gate on $|11\rangle$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Population evolution of states $|0110\rangle$, $|0020\rangle$, and $|0200\rangle$ over 500 ns under modulated coupler flux, demonstrating the parametric resonant interaction between $|0110\rangle$ and $|0020\rangle$.

fields.result: DPMZM architecture provides an SNR enhancement of approximately $6\,\mathrm{dB}$ over conventional MZM in NG-PON2, improving BPSK BER by nearly five orders of magnitude at $N_{s}=1$.
fields.question: Can quantum detection integrated with a dual-parallel Mach-Zehnder modulator architecture improve receiver sensitivity and error rates over standard MZM configurations in NG-PON2?
fields.prior: Baseline MZM-based NG-PON2 quantum communication systems using classical or basic MZM modulation.
fields.limits: Numerical simulation and analytical model assuming shot-noise-limited detection; excludes detector loss, electronic noise, phase noise, timing jitter, and finite ADC resolution.
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 2: SNR versus average number of signal photons $N_{s}$ for MZM-based and DPMZM-based NG-PON2 communication systems.
fields.figure_gloss: SNR plotted against average received signal photon number $N_{s}$, showing an approximate $6\,\mathrm{dB}$ gain for the DPMZM system over the conventional MZM architecture across the entire range.

fields.result: Differential Rydberg atomic receiver with local-oscillator phase balancing and inter-cell noise correlation achieves up to ~10 dB SNR gain as photon shot noise correlation approaches unity, requiring $-154.5$ dBm minimum detectable power at 0 dB threshold SNR.
fields.question: Can phase-balanced differential detection across coupled Rydberg vapor cells suppress quantum and optical shot noise to detect weak GNSS signals?
fields.prior: Conventional single-cell RAQR required $-146$ dBm, 20-ms coherent HS-GNSS required $-133$ dBm, and conventional GNSS receiver required $-120$ dBm under identical 0 dB threshold SNR conditions.
fields.limits: Theoretical and simulated only; assumes perfect cell matching, precise LO phase balancing, and sustained inter-cell quantum projection and photon shot noise correlations without implementation losses or phase errors.
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 4: Minimum power $P_{b}^{(\min)}$ versus (a) $P_{\rm out}^{(\max)}$ and (b) $\gamma_{\rm th}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Minimum detectable power $P_b^{(\min)}$ plotted against maximum outage probability $P_{\rm out}^{(\max)}$ and threshold SNR $\gamma_{\rm th}$, showing differential receiver outperforming conventional RAQR and classical GNSS architectures by 8.5 dB to 34.5 dB.

fields.result: Practical discrete-variable QKD secret key rates track theoretical finite-key bounds closely up to 40 km, with Cascade and Polar code reconciliation extending reach to ~55 km while LDPC cuts off near 45 km.
fields.question: How do practical post-processing implementations of Cascade, Winnow, LDPC, and Polar codes compare against theoretical asymptotic and finite-key secret key rate bounds across realistic discrete-variable QKD channel conditions?
fields.limits: Simulated fiber transmission; discrete-variable BB84 with weak coherent pulses (mean photon number $\mu \approx 0.1$ to $0.15$); all protocols yield zero secret key rate for measured QBER $\ge 11\%$ or $\mu \ge 0.2$ at 40 km.
tools: Belief propagation with OSD-0 decoding (5G NR LDPC)
Toeplitz hashing and SHAKE256 privacy amplification
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 9 : Secret key rate $R_{\mathrm{sk}}$ versus fiber transmission distance $d$ (km), comparing the client-server BB84 post-processing protocols against theoretical asymptotic and finite-key BB84 bounds.
fields.figure_gloss: Secret key rate $R_{\mathrm{sk}}$ versus fiber transmission distance $d$ in km. Shows Cascade, Polar, LDPC, and Winnow post-processing curves tracking below asymptotic and finite-key theoretical BB84 bounds until dropping to zero between 45 km and 55 km.

fields.result: Parallel shuttling minimizes decoherence and leakage at short shuttling distances, whereas sequential shuttling outperforms it over long distances across 2-, 3-, and 4-spin encodings; multi-spin fidelity loss and leakage decompose analytically into sums of at most seven pairwise spin error parameters $\epsilon_{jk}^{P}$.
fields.question: How do spatial and temporal correlations in magnetic noise affect dephasing and leakage during the shuttling of multi-spin logical qubits across different trajectories?
fields.limits: Pure dephasing via rotating-frame secular Hamiltonian (neglecting $x,y$ noise and spin relaxation). Neglects inter-spin exchange interaction during shuttling. Assumes stationary, isotropic Gaussian noise field.
tools: Gaussian random field model of spatio-temporal $1/f$ noise

(d)–(f) : Dependence of the spin-pair errors $\epsilon_{s}$ , $\epsilon^{\prime}_{s}$ , $\epsilon_{p}$ , $\epsilon^{\prime}_{p}$ , and $\epsilon_{d}$ on the dimensionless shuttling length $\lambda$ . The panels correspond to the same values $\delta=0.3$ , $0.4$ , and $0.8$ as panels (a)–(c). In all panels, $u=2.0$ and $\ell=2.0$ , the other parameters are given in Table 1 .

Parallel shuttling yields lower error at short range, whereas sequential shuttling wins at long range.

fields.result: Raman-coupled 1D Bose lattice gases with imbalanced interactions realize a Raman anyon-Hubbard model exhibiting chiral interactions with unbounded statistical phase $\theta$, supporting chiral bound states whose energy gap grows monotonically with $\theta$.
fields.question: Can a 1D lattice model exhibiting many-body anyonic physics be realized with ultracold atoms without Floquet driving?
fields.prior: Floquet-engineered anyon-Hubbard implementations were restricted to a truncated two-particle Fock space with heating-limited coherence times.
fields.limits: Requires large band gap $\Omega \gg t, U_{\sigma\sigma'}$, low density to neglect three-body terms, and small next-to-nearest neighbor tunneling $t_2 \ll t_1$.
fields.figure_caption: FIG. 4: Chiral bound states of the Raman anyon-Hubbard model. (a) Two-particle spectrum $E_{q}$ of the RAHM ( 7 ) at $U_{\mathrm{eff}}=0$ as a function of the center-of-mass momentum $q$ , obtained by truncating the interparticle distance to $r_{\mathrm{max}}=100$ . Colored dots show the upper and lower bound-state branches at $\theta=0.1\pi$ (orange), $0.2\pi$ (red) and $0.3\pi$ (purple), and crosses of the same color the corresponding results for the AHM ( 8 ). (b) Binding energy $\Delta_{\mathrm{g}}$ (upper panel) and inverse mean interparticle distance $r_{\mathrm{mean}}^{-1}$ (lower panel) of the lowest two-particle eigenstate as a function of $q$ , extrapolated to $r_{\mathrm{max}}\rightarrow\infty$ . Both quantities vanish for $\theta=0$ (gray dotted line). (c) Two-particle spectrum of the flux ladder model ( 1 ) for $\Omega=100t$ (left) and $\Omega=20t$ (right), obtained with $r_{\mathrm{max}}=50$ . Blue dots mark its bound states, which detach from the scattering continuum (gray), and light crosses show the RAHM supplemented by the second-neighbor tunneling $t_{2}$ of Appendix A . In both cases, $\delta=0$ , and $\gamma$ and $U_{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}$ are adjusted to give $\theta=0.25\pi$ , $U_{\mathrm{eff}}=0$ and $t_{2}=-0.1t_{1}$ , so that the RAHM results, which depend only on $\theta$ and $t_{2}/t_{1}$ , are the same in both panels. Energies are scaled to $t_{1}$ , and only the lower-band sector of the spectrum is shown. (d) Full two-particle spectrum of the noninteracting flux ladder at $\Omega=20t$ and $\gamma=0.73\pi$ . (e) $r_{\mathrm{mean}}^{-1}$ of the lowest two-particle eigenstate for the flux ladder and the RAHM with the parameters of (c). At $U_{\mathrm{eff}}=0$ , the statistical interactions alone bind the particles into two branches, below and above the scattering continuum, which exist only for $q\gtrsim\pi$ : the lower branch has only negative group velocities $\mathrm{d}E_{q}/\mathrm{d}q$ , the upper one only positive ones (a). Their gap grows with $\theta$ and exceeds that of the AHM at $\theta=0.3\pi$ (b). These chiral bound states persist in the flux ladder even at $\Omega=20t$ (c,e), where the interaction energies approach the band gap.
fields.figure_gloss: Two-particle energy spectrum $E_q$ as a function of center-of-mass momentum $q$ for $U_{\mathrm{eff}}=0$. The continuum of scattering states is flanked by upper and lower chiral bound state bands separated by an energy gap that increases with $\theta$.

fields.result: Amplitude-encoding state preparation simplifies multiplexer circuits to 1- and 2-qubit gates, reducing circuit depth by up to orders of magnitude at equivalent state fidelity compared to standard multiplexer methods.
fields.question: How can generic high-dimensional complex data or queryable functions be deterministically loaded into quantum states without exponential memory or circuit-depth overhead?
fields.prior: Möttönen multiplexer-based state preparation decomposed generic states in $\Theta(N/n)$ depth via Shende recursive trees (as implemented in Qiskit), requiring dense storage of $2(2^n - 1)$ angles.
fields.limits: Boolean simplification involves an NP-hard optimization problem; Walsh-Hadamard method requires one clean ancilla qubit; memory reduction to $O(2l\chi^2)$ relies on low Matrix Product State bond dimension $\chi$.
tools: Tensor Train / Matrix Product State representation
Boolean logic Disjoint Sum of Products minimization
fields.figure_caption: Figure 12 : Ratio of the CX-depth of each Binary-Tree method to that of Qiskit’s state-preparation circuit as a function of the number of data qubits $n$ , replotting the data from Fig. 11 . Panels (a), (b), and (c) correspond to the methods Binary-Tree Boolean Encoder, Binary-Tree Walsh–Hadamard Transform, BT-Hybrid, respectively. The function-family legend is provided in Table 2 . We see that for most function families, BT-WHT beats qiskit by $n=15$ , and when including BT-BE to construct a BT-Hybrid, it beats Qiskit for every function family.
fields.figure_gloss: Ratio of CX-depth of the proposed Binary-Tree methods (BT-BE, BT-WHT, BT-Hybrid) to Qiskit's state-preparation circuit depth plotted against qubit count $n$ across various target function families, demonstrating depth reductions of several orders of magnitude.

fields.result: Factoring RSA-2048 uses $5.08\times 10^{9}$ Toffoli gates at $1{,}461$ peak logical qubits ($15\%$ reduction) and $2.55\times 10^{9}$ Toffoli gates at $1{,}806$ qubits ($46\%$ reduction).
fields.question: How many logical qubits and Toffoli gates are required to factor an RSA-2048 key when optimizing residue-arithmetic modular exponentiation?
fields.prior: was $5.98\times 10^{9}$ Toffolis at 1,461 qubits and $4.74\times 10^{9}$ at 1,806 qubits (Gidney 2025)
fields.limits: Logical-circuit counts obtained via simulation; physical qubit and runtime projections depend on architecture-specific routing and compilation models without full layout validation.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Fewest Toffoli gates per RSA-2048 factoring for a given number of logical qubits. Grey: the reference circuit at its best parameter setting for each qubit count (the published cost model, which favours the reference circuit). Blue: our circuits (measured); filled dots mark Pareto circuits and open diamonds mark the no-sharing ablations. Labels A–E match Table 1 . The shaded area is the saving; the grey square is the published configuration in its original model.
fields.figure_gloss: Fewest Toffoli gates per RSA-2048 factoring plotted against peak logical-qubit count. Blue points denote the new circuits and grey denotes the reference circuit evaluated across 534,240 parameter settings.

fields.result: Twisted compactification corresponds directly to quotient quantum codes; for 3D fermionic toric codes under a quarter-turn twist, it yields codes with linear distance starting at $[[768,2,9]]$ hosting an explicit $p+ip$ pump that acts logically as $T$ up to Clifford factors.
fields.question: How do topological twisted compactifications map systematically onto quotient quantum error-correcting codes, their logical operators, and their transversal gates?
fields.limits: Finite regular covers are required to describe the dressed Gauss laws as quotients. Invertible abelian gauge theories under twisting reach only quantum doubles $D(G)$ with $[G,G]$ central.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: The quarter-turn space $M=T^{2}_{L}\rtimes_{C_{4}}S^{1}$ of Proposition 4.24 (schematic). (a) A fundamental domain: the fibre square, with opposite sides identified, times the $J$ layers of the circle. The top face is glued to the bottom face after a quarter turn, $(x,y,0)\sim(-y,x,J)$ , so the two arrows are identified. (b) The two membranes of Table 4 : a fibre, and the cross $\{x=0\}\cup\{y=0\}$ swept around the circle, which closes up because the quarter turn maps the cross to itself. (c) Two kinds of logical strings. The rotation axis is a closed loop of length $J$ that winds once around the circle; the lightest logical operators of Table 4 are strings of this kind. A fibre cycle is the torsion class of $H_{1}(M;{\mathbb{Z}})={\mathbb{Z}}\oplus{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}$ : twice it bounds, and the linking form on this torsion gives the cubic term $\int\tau^{3}$ behind the logical $T$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Fundamental domain geometry of the quarter-turn compactified mapping torus $T^{2}_{L}times_{C_{4}}S^{1}$, whose quotient yields codes hosting the logical $T$ gate via a $p+ip$ pump.

fields.result: 192 explicit binary stabilizer codes with $53\le n\le 254$ and $5\le d\le 13$ exceed the lower distance bounds in Grassl's tables, raising 1,873 table entries by standard propagation rules. Expurgated random codes yield roughly 8 more logical qubits than typical random codes.
fields.question: Can random stabilizer codes improved by expurgation beat the best known lower bounds recorded in Grassl's qubit code tables?
fields.prior: Grassl's tables (as of 4 November 2026); 161 codes beat the table's distance by 1 and 31 beat it by 2, yielding gains of up to 9 logical qubits at fixed $(n,d)$ where the table was near the Gilbert-Varshamov bound.
fields.limits: Certifying distance requires exhaustively checking up to $4.2\times 10^{13}$ Pauli operators, scaling in time and memory as $n^{d/2}$ (requiring supercomputer clusters for $n\approx 250, d\approx 13$); codes have dense check matrices.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Number of stabilizer generators $n-k$ needed at length $n$ for distance $d$ ; lower is better, and at fixed $(n,d)$ a vertical step of one is one logical qubit. Solid gray: quantum Singleton bound $n-k\geq 2(d-1)$ . Dotted gray: random-code (Gilbert–Varshamov) level $n-k_{\rm rand}(n,d)$ . Blue: best code in Grassl’s table [ 1 ] , read on 4 November 2026. Dashed orange: the calibrated predictor of Sec. III for random encoders with expurgation. Orange dots: the 192 new codes. Where the blue line lies above the orange dashed one, the predictor expects random encoders with expurgation to improve the table.
fields.figure_gloss: Plots generator count $n-k$ versus code length $n$ across distances $d=5$ to 13. Shows the 192 new codes beating the existing table entries in regions where the table codes matched the Gilbert-Varshamov bound.

fields.result: Recovering exact Hamming weight and computing any symmetric Boolean function takes at most $n/2 + O(n^{1/3})$ quantum queries with bounded error; explicit symmetric functions require $n/2 + \Omega(n^{1/3})$ queries.
fields.question: Is any additive overhead beyond $n/2$ unavoidable for quantum query algorithms computing a single Boolean output, and what is its optimal worst-case order?
fields.prior: was $n/2 + O(\sqrt{n})$ queries for all Boolean functions via oracle interrogation (van Dam 1998)
fields.limits: Worst-case query complexity; bounded constant error; lower bound proven for symmetric Boolean functions.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Each square represents one hamming weight. In (a), $F_{2m,0}$ is zero on the two central layers $m-1,m$ and alternates on either side. In (b), every layer from $m-R-1$ through $m+R$ has output zero.
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic of the symmetric functions $F_{2m,0}$ and $F_{2m,R}$ across input Hamming weights, highlighting the central zero-valued plateaus of width 2 and $2R+2$ adjacent to alternating tail regions.

fields.result: Non-resonant LZSM interferometry driven by STM bias voltage achieves coherent remote spin flips of a Ti atom coupled to Fe with 97.3% to 99.3% inversion probability in 14.2 ns to 19.8 ns, leaving the Ti spin directly under the tip unchanged.
fields.question: Can quantum interference from non-resonant driving flip a remote atomic spin while protecting it from STM tunneling-electron decoherence?
fields.limits: Numerical simulation assuming fast-driving regime $\delta \ll 1$; Ti-Ti-Fe trimer on MgO/Ag; neglects dipolar coupling relative to exchange; does not simulate explicit dissipation or bath dynamics.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 6: Time evolution LZSM transition between diabatic states, $|--Fe\rangle\rightarrow|-+Fe\rangle$ for the trimer with $J_{t}=0.6$ GHz and $J_{f}=6.8$ GHz, $d_{\rm tip}=0.6$ nm, $B_{\rm ext}=0.497$ T. fields.result: Proves an $O(1)$ circuit-level threshold under local stochastic noise for fault-tolerant quantum memory in any 2D non-chiral topological phase, preserving logical info for a quasi-stretched-exponential time in system size.
fields.question: Can quantum memory and logical operations be realized fault-tolerantly with a provable circuit-level threshold for arbitrary, non-solvable non-abelian topological phases?
fields.prior: Ref. [17] sketched a threshold proof for an RG decoder restricted to non-cyclic anyon models under phenomenological noise without microscopic circuits; thresholds were previously proven only for solvable quantum doubles like $D_4$ and $S_3$.
fields.limits: Restricted to 2D non-chiral topological orders. Assumes classical processing is fast and cheap, and syndrome measurements are deterministic in absence of noise.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: (a) A syndrome line starting from a $k$ -burst $B$ . (b,c) Illustration of conglomerates. Bursts are drawn as gray boxes, anyon worldlines are drawn as blue lines, and cluster boxes for non-dominant bursts are shown as dashed purple outlines. None of the three level- $k$ bursts in (b) are dominant as their cluster boxes overlap with anyon worldlines originating at the level- $>k$ burst.

fields.result: Autler-Townes microwave drive on $|2angle 	o |3angle$ transition tunes effective qubit anharmonicity without degrading coherence, demonstrating a 97 ns non-adiabatic CZ gate with 99.40(9)% fidelity.
fields.question: Can high-fidelity, fast entangling gates be realized in superconducting circuits with all-microwave drives without trading off gate speed for leakage or degrading coherence through frequency tuning?
fields.limits: Static decoherence accounts for ~78% of the CZ gate error; off-resonant drive introduces a ~2 MHz frequency drift requiring virtual-Z frame corrections.

fields.result: Realized continuous superconducting Pb films extending seamlessly from selective-area-grown PbTe nanowires onto the CdTe substrate with an atomically sharp, in situ-equivalent interface. Thermal annealing at 340 ∘ C cleanly desorbs a sacrificial protective Te capping layer following ex situ dielectric mask removal.
fields.question: How can a continuous superconducting film be deposited across a PbTe nanowire and the substrate without introducing disorder from the dielectric mask?
fields.limits: Ultrasonic mask peel-off relies on convergence with auxiliary segmented lines over CdTe undercut regions; Te layer removal requires a short Ar treatment followed by 60 min annealing at 340 ∘ C.

(c) Removal of Si 3 N 4 dielectric mask and fabrication of shadow walls. (d) Decomposition of the Te layer. (e) Deposition of Pb film and CdTe capping (not shown). fields.result: Hexagonal germanium's top bulk valence band has vanishing in-plane $g$ factors ($g_{xx}=g_{yy}=0$) by symmetry, leaving only $|g_{zz}|	hickapprox 18.08$. Confined nanowires retain this strong anisotropy with $|g_{xx}|,|g_{yy}|	hinspaceaisebox{-0.5ex}{$ uildrel<	hicksim elow$}	hinspace 1$, while a transverse electric field yields Rashba coupling up to $\alpha_R\thickapprox 16\text{ meV nm}$ and spin-orbit length down to $\approx 60\text{ nm}$.
fields.question: How do quantum confinement, magnetic fields, and transverse electric fields determine the effective $g$-tensor and Rashba spin-orbit coupling of holes in hexagonal germanium nanowires?
fields.prior: Prior work (Wang et al. 2021) incorrectly took the bulk transverse hole $g$-factor to be the bare electron value 2 because of phase inconsistencies in the ten-band $\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{p}$ Hamiltonian.
fields.limits: Square nanowires with side length $20\text{ nm} \le L \le 60\text{ nm}$, hard-wall boundaries, low-energy regime near $\Gamma$, electric fields below $\approx 10\text{ V}/\mu\text{m}$ (where Stark effect collapses the direct bandgap).
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Electric-field dependence and anisotropy of the effective Rashba coefficient for a hexagonal germanium nanowire. (a),(b) Variation of $\alpha_{R}$ as a function of electric fields applied along $y$ and $z$ , respectively. (c) Polar representation of $\alpha_{R}$ for a field rotated in the $yz$ plane at fixed magnitudes in the range $1\,\mathrm{V}/\mu\mathrm{m}\leq\mathcal{E}\leq 7\,\mathrm{V}/\mu\mathrm{m}$ . The angles $\theta=0^{\circ}$ and $90^{\circ}$ correspond to $\bm{\mathcal{E}}\parallel+z$ and $\bm{\mathcal{E}}\parallel+y$ , respectively. Progressively darker blue curves denote increasing field strength. For all panels, the side length of the square cross section of the nanowire is $L=30~\mathrm{nm}$ .

Demonstrates nonlinear field dependence and orders-of-magnitude stronger Rashba coupling when the electric field is perpendicular to the crystal $c$ axis ($y$ direction).

fields.result: Differential testing framework finds 6 instability sources across Qiskit, Cirq, and Pyquil (4 crash bugs, 2 root causes explaining 25 of 29 hardware divergences) while static circuit filtering reduces backend runs by 66%.
fields.question: How to differentially test quantum software stacks across compilers, simulators, and hardware despite probabilistic outputs and severe execution costs?
fields.limits: Evaluated on at most 5 qubits without quantum error correction; total fuzzing run time capped at seven days.

fields.result: Crosstalk-induced quantum row hammer attacks flip victim qubit measurement outcomes by up to $60\%$, degrading $2\rightarrow 1$ quantum random access code retrieval success probability from 0.8484 to 0.4751.
fields.question: To what extent do crosstalk-induced quantum row hammer attacks persist across different quantum processors, and do devices with identical connectivity graphs exhibit comparable vulnerability profiles?
fields.limits: Attacks applied via cloud-based shared access; circuits run with 40,000 shots on IBM, 8,000 on IQM, and 10,000 on QRAC experiments; QRAC tests evaluated exclusively on IBM Marrakesh.
tools: superconducting quantum processors (IBM Fez, Kingston, Marrakesh, Pittsburgh, Boston, Miami; IQM Garnet)
bidirectional CNOT sequences on neighboring hammer qubits
quantum random access codes ($2\rightarrow 1$ and $3\rightarrow 1$ QRACs)
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Measured crosstalk-induced bias for IBM quantum processors sharing the connectivity graph shown in Fig. 1 . Despite possessing identical coupling topologies and being subjected to the same 30-CNOT attack configuration, the devices exhibit different attack strengths and distributions. Blue bars represent the probability of measuring the victim qubit in the state $\ket{1}$ under attack, while green dashed lines indicate the control precision obtained from the corresponding control experiments.
fields.figure_gloss: Measured crosstalk-induced flip probability on victim qubits across five IBM heavy-hex processors compared to control idle readouts. Demonstrates large variations in attack susceptibility across devices despite identical coupling topologies.

fields.result: Stabilizer repetition-code process tomography under fixed measurement bases achieves full Jacobian rank using only 0, 1, and 5 recovery Pauli gates for $n=3, 5, 7$ qubits, whereas full minimum-weight decoding requires 6, 50, and 308 gates.
fields.question: How many physical single-qubit Pauli gates does a repetition-code decoder need to preserve parameter information during process tomography?
fields.prior: Full minimum-weight decoding required 6, 50, and 308 gates for $n=3, 5, 7$ qubits (giving only rank 24/27 at $n=7$); first-order decoding required 6, 10, and 14 gates.
fields.limits: Restricted to single-qubit Pauli recovery gates within minimum-weight error representatives; requires fixed 16-element measurement setting table; does not account for mid-circuit measurement latency, circuit depth, or leakage.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Precision against recovery-gate count, medians over the working points. (a) $n=3$ : the curve is U-shaped with a minimum at three gates; the standard six-gate decoder is $9.5$ times worse at the median, and worse at every point ( $1.8$ to $88$ times). (b) $n=5$ : a broad plateau around six gates, but the whole curve, floor included, lies two to three decades above the $10$ mrad target on every platform. Filled markers are the quoted designs.
fields.figure_gloss: Precision versus total recovery-gate count across sampled working points. For $n=3$, precision shows a U-shaped dependence minimizing at three gates, beating the standard six-gate decoder by a factor of 9.5 at the median.

fields.result: Discovers and formally verifies quantum circuits across 5 benchmarks, lowering logical spacetime volume $Q\cdot\mathcal{T}$ up to 290x for arithmetic and 2.5x to 11x for large-scale scientific simulations.
fields.question: Can multi-agent LLM systems automatically discover and formally verify resource-reduced quantum algorithms at scales beyond classical simulation?
fields.prior: For cytochrome P450, prior compiled baseline was $Q_{\text{base}}\cdot\mathcal{T}_{\text{base}} = 1.09\times 10^{12}$ ($Q=481$, $\mathcal{T}=2.26\times 10^9$).
fields.limits: Circuits and proofs target fault-tolerant architectures counting logical qubits and $T$ gates ($Q\cdot\mathcal{T}$); assumes idealized clean ancilla reset and exact/bounded-error synthesis without physical noise models.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Summary of verified results. a) Quantum algorithm cost for baselines and solutions from this work across application domains. b) Logical-qubit and $T$ -gate improvements on the three scientific applications, with feathered hardware horizons (dashed lines at geometric midpoints) for medium-term fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC † ; teraquop planar architectures [ 208 , 154 ] ) and application-scale FTQC ‡ (fault-tolerant application-scale quantum computers, FASQ [ 149 , 148 , 208 ] ). Grey points denote published baselines, red points denote refined baselines incorporating subsequent methodological improvements from the literature, and blue points denote this work. For cytochrome P450, the published ground-state estimate is extended to all eigenstates within $0.1$ Ha of $E_{0}$ , raising its cost by $0.85\%$ . c) Cost for $25$ -bit fixed-point $\arcsin$ ( $\varepsilon\leq 1.25\times 10^{-7}$ ) against piecewise-polynomial evaluation [ 157 ] . d) Speedup in expected number of rounds for large $N$ of our verified parallel Grover circuits over the strongest published baseline [ 209 , 210 , 211 , 212 , 213 ] for powers of two $m,k\leq 2^{10}$ when finding any one or all of $k$ marked targets with $m$ parallel queries per round (dashed contours: $1.00\times$ boundary; $*$ markers: peak speedups of $1.22\times$ and $1.41\times$ ).
fields.figure_gloss: Resource costs for quantum algorithms across applications comparing prior baselines against verified discovered circuits, showing logical qubit and $T$-gate reductions.

fields.result: Machine-learning surrogates compress quantum randomized-measurement data to bypass classical shadow postprocessing, enabling chemically accurate quantum-classical QMC on up to 40 qubits with 190-fold to 4,100-fold speedups.
fields.question: How can the computational bottleneck of repeatedly reconstructing quantum trial-state overlaps from classical shadows during quantum Monte Carlo propagation be overcome?
fields.prior: Hardware demonstrations of quantum-classical QMC were limited to 16 qubits and required over 13,000 GPU hours for a single calculation; 40-qubit postprocessing was estimated to take millions of CPU hours.
fields.limits: Requires training determinants $N_{\mathrm{train}} \ll N_{\mathrm{w}} N_{\tau}$; training stopped via experimental noise floor $F$ to avoid overfitting finite measurement noise.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Accurate and accelerated QC-QMC using experimental randomized measurements. a . Quantum circuit: a GHZ-type state is prepared on the $\alpha$ (spin-up) and $\beta$ (spin-down) registers. Independent random matchgate circuits then act on each register before computational-basis measurements. The lower diagram illustrates the decomposition of a matchgate block into single-qubit Clifford and CZ gates. b . QC-QMC energy deviations from the noiseless, infinite-shot reference for hydrogen chains from $\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{4}}}$ to $\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{20}}}$ (8 to 40 qubits) at an interatomic separation of $3.0$ Bohr in the STO-6G basis. Results from conventional shadow postprocessing (red) are compared with those from the ML surrogate (blue). The shaded region indicates chemical accuracy ( $\pm 1$ kcal mol -1 ). ML results are averaged over independently trained models (Fig. S3.6 ), with error bars indicating standard errors of the mean, including reference uncertainty. c . Total classical computational cost of conventional QC-QMC and our ML-accelerated approach. At 8 and 16 qubits, both methods use the same quantum measurement data, yielding speedups of 190- and 4,100-fold, respectively. The ML costs include training-label generation, surrogate training, and QMC propagation. The inset shows the total number of measurement snapshots (circuits $\times$ shots) used at each system size (Supplementary Table S1.1 ).
fields.figure_gloss: Energy error relative to infinite-shot reference versus qubit count (8 to 40 qubits) for hydrogen chains (b), and total classical CPU/GPU cost for brute-force shadow processing versus ML surrogate showing 190- to 4,100-fold speedups (c).

fields.result: NP search problems solved with unit success probability in $O(\sqrt{N/M})$ oracle queries using verifier-based reversible quantum circuits requiring $O(\mathrm{poly}(n))$ qubits.
fields.question: How can quantum search deterministically identify satisfying assignments for general NP problems directly from their classical polynomial-time verifiers without losing the quadratic query speedup?
fields.limits: Requires exact prior knowledge of the number of valid solutions $M$ (or the initial success probability); ideal state-vector simulation without noise.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3 : Simulated probability for the four-variable 4-SAT instance after three deterministic search iterations. The state 1101 , corresponding to the unique satisfying assignment $x_{3}x_{2}x_{1}x_{0}=1101$ , has unit probability.
fields.figure_gloss: Measured state probability for a 4-variable 4-SAT instance after 3 calibrated iterations. The single valid assignment 1101 is found with probability exactly 1.0.

fields.result: Synthesizes robust single-qubit control pulses with a mean local optimization time of 39.945 ms per gate across 2,000 rotations, yielding nominal gate infidelities below $10^{-9}$ (mean $5.526\times 10^{-10}$) after virtual phase correction.
fields.question: Can dynamically corrected, robust quantum gates be synthesized computationally fast enough to allow on-demand generation at compile time?
fields.prior: Synthesizing dynamically corrected gates via numerical optimization such as BARQ in qurveros took on the order of minutes per gate.
fields.limits: Single-qubit gates only; noise model assumes quasistatic multiplicative amplitude and additive detuning errors; times exclude offline preparation of reference and continuation library; infidelities require ideal virtual phase correction on a 1,000-interval discretization.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Optimizer time for each of the 2,000 interpolation-initialized queries on $[0,\pi]$ . Cross markers indicate individual queries, with a logarithmic time axis. All queries were accepted. Times measure the optimizer call only and exclude reference and library preparation.
fields.figure_gloss: Optimizer execution time (logarithmic scale) for 2,000 single-qubit rotations as a function of the target rotation angle $\theta \in [0, \pi]$. Local optimization times mostly cluster in the tens of milliseconds across the entire angular range.

fields.result: Boron nitride nanotubes host multiple room-temperature single-photon emitters along a single tube spanning the entire visible spectrum, with lifetimes down to 0.5 ns.
fields.question: Can boron nitride nanotubes host stable room-temperature single-photon emitters suitable for nanophotonic integration?
fields.prior: Fastest hBN single-photon emitter lifetimes were roughly twofold slower (around 1 ns).
fields.limits: Room temperature; tested on tubes with radius ~25 nm; blinking mitigated by surface coating.

fields.result: Discovered negative non-linear differential dissipation in a 32.7 kHz quartz tuning fork at temperatures below 0.3 K, where strong driving suppresses mechanical loss.
fields.question: What mechanisms dominate the amplitude- and temperature-dependent dissipation in high-Q low-frequency quartz resonators in vacuum at millikelvin temperatures?
fields.limits: Observed below 0.3 K in high vacuum; requires high oscillation amplitude and excess microwave noise from the readout preamplifier.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Total relaxation rate measured from ring-down experiments at temperatures $T=$ $41000\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{K}$ . The inset denotes the oscillation amplitude in terms of the read-out current $I_{\mathrm{t}}$ for each of the nine data sets. The overlaid curves are derived from Eq. ( 11 ) using a procedure described in Appendix C . The resonant absorption is suppressed at high oscillation amplitude (large $I_{\mathrm{t}}$ ), leaving the relaxation absorption to dominate.
fields.figure_gloss: Mechanical relaxation rate versus temperature from 4 mK to 1000 mK measured at nine distinct oscillation amplitudes. Higher oscillation amplitudes suppress the low-temperature resonant loss peak, fitting the interacting TLS bath model.

fields.result: Compiler pfoqcompiler merges compatible recursive calls across quantum branches in $\mathrm{FOQ}$. Produces polynomial-size circuits for weakly well-founded bounded-width programs and polylogarithmic depth under weak recursive halving, removing asymptotic sequentialization overhead without exponential ancilla overhead.
fields.question: Can recursive quantum control in first-order quantum languages be compiled into parallelized circuits without incurring exponential ancillary qubit overhead or exponential circuit depth?
fields.prior: Naive compilation yields exponential circuit depth from sequentializing branches; standard parallelization techniques require an exponential number of ancillary qubits.
fields.limits: Applies to FOQ programs satisfying syntactically checkable weak well-foundedness, bounded width, and weak uniformity/halving conditions.
tools: syntactic analysis of recursive halving and uniformity

fields.result: Introduces QASC, translating OpenQASM3.0 classical control and circuits into C++ linked to QuEST, plus QACC-perf, which estimates HPC-QPU offloading communication latencies ranging from 0.084 ms on-node to 2718.000 ms over cloud across molecular circuits up to 50.3 MB.
fields.question: How can OpenQASM3.0 programs with complex classical control be efficiently simulated and their HPC–quantum computing integration performance quantitatively modelled?
fields.limits: Does not support OpenQASM3.0 gate calibration, physical qubits, pragmas, or annotations; performance model tested via simulation rather than physical QPU hardware.
fields.figure_gloss: Communication overhead in ms against circuit size in MB across on-node, multi-node, and cloud integration modes, alongside transpilation-to-execution runtime ratios across tested molecular system sizes.

fields.result: Multiparticle neutrino oscillations converge to Boltzmann-type mean-field kinetic solutions as particle number $N$ grows, with RMS residuals declining towards zero up to $N = 1\,300\,000$. Mean-field breakdown requires non-mean-field conditions like linear streams with overlapping wave packets or chained once-in-a-lifetime encounters.
fields.question: Does quantum entanglement survive to invalidate mean-field quantum kinetic equations for collective neutrino oscillations in dense astrophysical environments as the number of neutrinos grows large?
fields.limits: Demonstrated analytically and numerically on two-mode toy systems (electron-muon and neutrino-antineutrino bipolar oscillations); full astrophysical environments are three-dimensional, turbulent, and multi-scale.
tools: Trotterized quantum simulation circuit with Draper adder
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Comparison of the quantum kinetic mean-field treatment of collective neutrino oscillations (black curves, see Section 2.1 ) to the results of full multiparticle simulations (see Section 3 ) on classical hardware (purple curves) and on a superconducting transmon quantum processor (blue data points). The blue dashed line correspond to a noiseless simulation of the Trotterized quantum circuit. Top: a two-mode system with initially $N$ electron neutrinos and $N$ muon neutrinos, exhibiting both slow and fast oscillations. Middle: bipolar oscillations in a system with $N$ neutrinos and $N$ antineutrinos. Bottom: root-mean-square residuals between the quantum kinetic mean-field results and the multiparticle simulation as a function of the number of neutrinos per mode.
fields.figure_gloss: Flavor survival probability vs. dimensionless time and root-mean-square residuals vs. particle number per mode $N$. Demonstrates convergence of full multiparticle classical and quantum processor simulations to the quantum kinetic mean-field limit as $N$ increases.

fields.result: Survey categorizes quantum knowledge distillation across C2Q, Q2Q, Q2C, and quantum-enhanced configurations. Experimental benefits remain task- and architecture-dependent, with several studies reporting negligible gains or degradation, and hardware demonstrations rarely testing full learning pipelines.
fields.question: How do quantum knowledge distillation frameworks transfer supervisory signals across classical, quantum, and hybrid models, and what experimental evidence exists for their performance and resource advantages?
fields.limits: Few hardware evaluations; inconsistent baseline matching; prevalent noiseless simulation; attribution confounded by encoding and ansatz design choices.
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 2: Combinations of teacher-student configurations in quantum knowledge distillation.
fields.figure_gloss: Taxonomy of knowledge transfer configurations linking classical and quantum teachers and students, alongside quantum-enhanced setups.

fields.result: Optimal control yields near-ideal work across a quantum critical point on stroke durations growing linearly with system size $\tau^{\mathrm{thrs}}_{N} \propto N$, replacing the $N^2$ scaling of linear driving. Above a crossover system size, maximum cycle power is achieved on a fast, size-independent branch that trades work for shorter cycle time.
fields.question: How can finite-time unitary strokes and endpoint energy scales be jointly optimized to maximize power in a many-body quantum Otto engine crossing a quantum critical point?
fields.prior: Linear ramps require stroke durations scaling quadratically with system size $\tau \propto N^2$ to suppress nonadiabatic excitations across the critical point.
fields.limits: Complete thermalization strokes of fixed duration, 1D nearest-neighbor transverse-field Ising chain, and zero apparatus energy overhead.
tools: transverse-field Ising chain mapping to free fermions
quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) optimal control
fields.figure_caption: Figure 8: Maximum cycle power as a function of the system size $N$ , for $2\tau_{\rm th}=5$ . (a) Unitary-stroke duration $\tau(\mathcal{P}_{\max})$ at which the power is maximal, for the optimized (circles) and linear (squares) protocols. The black dotted line is the fit of the threshold time, $\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{thrs}}_{N}$ , Eq. ( 68 ), and the gray dashed line is $\tau_{\mathrm{fast}}$ of Eq. ( 82 ). The durations are scanned with step $\Delta\tau_{\mathrm{un}}=1$ ; since the fast-branch maximum is flat, the values of $\tau(\mathcal{P}_{\max})$ are only indicative. (b) Maximum power per site. For the optimized protocol, circles show the maximum of the power obtained from the geometric mean of the residual energy over the $N_{\rm run}=10$ runs, and the shaded band spans the best and worst run at the same duration. The gray dashed and black dotted lines are the analytic fast- and slow-branch powers, Eqs. ( 83 ) and ( 85 ), the latter evaluated with the fit of $\tau^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{thrs}}_{N}$ . (c) Efficiency $\eta=W_{\mathrm{cycle}}/Q_{h}$ , Eq. ( 92 ), at the duration of maximum power, for the optimized (circles) and linear (squares) protocols; the shaded band spans the best and worst run at the same duration. The black dashed line is the ideal Otto efficiency $\eta^{\mathrm{id}}=1-g_{c}/J_{h}$ , reached when $e_{\mathrm{res}}=0$ , the gray dashed line is the fast-branch value $\eta_{\mathrm{fast}}=\eta(\tau_{\mathrm{fast}})$ , and the green solid line is the Curzon–Ahlborn efficiency [ 44 ] $\eta_{\rm CA}=1-\sqrt{T_{c}/T_{h}}$ , shown for reference. In all panels, the dash-dotted line labeled $N_{\times}$ marks $N_{\times}=36$ , the smallest size whose maximum power lies on the fast branch. This is consistent with the analytic estimate $N_{\times}\approx 34.4$ of Eq. ( 86 ). Times are in units of $\hbar/(k_{B}T_{h})$ and powers in units of $(k_{B}T_{h})^{2}/\hbar$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Stroke duration $\tau(\mathcal{P}_{\max})$ and maximum cycle power per site $\mathcal{P}_{\max}/N$ plotted versus system size $N$. Shows the transition from the slow branch matching ideal work to the fast, size-independent branch at $N \approx 36$ for the optimized protocol.

fields.result: Formulating quantum code and circuit distances as tropical partition functions enables certifying exact distances up to 31,200 qubits and circuits with $8\times 10^5$ fault mechanisms, uncovering overestimated distances across 10 of 26 recent papers.
fields.question: Can quantum code and circuit distances be exactly certified at the scale of practical low-density parity-check proposals rather than relying on heuristic upper bounds?
fields.prior: Existing exact solvers (integer programming, MaxSAT, connected-cluster enumeration) certify only small instances, leaving distances assumed: IBM's two-gross code was assumed circuit distance 18, now certified at 16 under its standard schedule.
fields.limits: Depolarizing noise model, identical noise on all live qubits in the chip study; exact runs on the two-gross code become significantly slower when defects break symmetry.
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 3: Published code and circuit distances against certified values. a , The 22 overestimated published values. Published values (open circles) are compared with certified values (blue circles) or intervals from proved lower bounds to the weights of the lightest errors found (blue bars). Orange lines mark the gaps; ticks mark code distances. Both values appear on the right ( $\leq$ , upper bound; $\approx$ , estimate or expectation). The repository entry is from the mitten repository. The $[\![288,12,18]\!]$ circuit appears with IBM’s bound and the best known value from the benchmark of distance methods. The $[\![2304,1156,16]\!]$ and $[\![2844,1426,18]\!]$ values are for the $Z$ basis at 8 cycles. Walking Cat and shift-automorphism values hold for all numberings of the check terms; values that depend on the numbering and circuits without published distances are not counted and appear only in Supplementary Table 8 . b , Previously unresolved distances, reported as conjectures, ranges (gray bars), lower bounds or best known values, now exact (blue points) or more tightly bounded (blue bars). Tanner and bivariate bicycle results come from longer runs outside the benchmark, described in Supplementary Section 6.5 ; published values are the best known value from the benchmark of distance methods. For Tanner codes, published and certified values are $Z$ distances; the tick marks the code distance 26 of $[\![396,4]\!]$ , its $X$ distance. c , Reconstructed surface-code circuits of ref. 47 , matching the published bounds. Diamonds and parenthesized values indicate alternative valid schedules. NZ and ZZ alternating are the two lifted schedules with alternating rounds. d , Fifteen modular hyperbolic color codes from Google’s study 47 , with previously unresolved distances certified at the upper endpoints of the published intervals; Supplementary Fig. 3 gives the constructions. Sources: mitten 14 , two-gross 11 , the benchmark of distance methods 9 (superdense, Tanner and bivariate bicycle rows), Cornucopia 13 , routing 15 , shift automorphism 16 , Walking Cat 18 , three-color 19 , vine 44 , amplified 45 , tile 46 , nearest-neighbor planar 29 , multivariate multicycle 25 , weight-8 bivariate bicycle 21 and modular hyperbolic 47 .
fields.figure_gloss: Published code and circuit distance estimates (open circles) compared against exact certified values (blue circles) or lower/upper bound intervals across 10 audited recent papers, showing overestimates by up to at least eight.

fields.result: Decomposing input Gram matrices over unpredictable subset partitions yields error-free subset discrimination with success probability equal to 1, even for non-orthogonal and linearly dependent states. For equidistant states, unit success holds when $\langle\varphi_i|\varphi_j\rangle = (N-2)/(2N-2)$.
fields.question: Can the success probability of error-free subset discrimination bypass standard limits and reach unity for non-orthogonal quantum states?
fields.prior: Subset discrimination and unambiguous state discrimination for non-orthogonal states strictly had success probability strictly below one for any fixed partition.
fields.limits: Restricted to pure states. Yields an unpredictable subset partition rather than a preselected one. Lacks an explicit cost-effective optical implementation and full finite-error security proof for the derived QKD protocol.

fields.result: Introduced Hamilton, a process calculus for Hamiltonian quantum computing. Semantics is fully abstract, equational theory is complete and decidable, and expressible Hamiltonians are precisely those with dyadic rational Pauli coefficients $m/2^k$.
fields.question: Can quantum programming treat continuous Hamiltonian evolution as an additive concurrent primitive with a sound, complete, and fully abstract equational calculus?
fields.prior: Circuit-level equational reasoning (like ZX phase gadgets or $\Pi_k$) handles unitaries at fixed precision but lacks an equational theory complete for Hamiltonians and their additive combinations.
fields.limits: Only targets first-order Lie-Trotter splittings; circuit emissions lack multi-qubit resynthesis/optimization (e.g. 18 CNOTs per step instead of 3); purely unitary with no dissipative dynamics, mid-circuit measurement, or block encoding.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 8. Probability $|a_{3}(t)|^{2}$ of finding the proton at $x_{3}=\ket{11}$ at time $t$ , starting there: exact evolution under $\tilde{H}$ (solid), and compiled circuits for $p$ with $k=12$ at refinement levels $n=2$ (dashed) and $n=4$ (dots). The probability of finding the proton at position x3, ket 11, after starting it there, over 40 femtoseconds. The exact curve oscillates between about 0.1 and 1; the points for n equal to 4 lie on it, and the dashed curve for n equal to 2 departs from it in places.
fields.figure_gloss: Survival probability $|a_3(t)|^2$ of a proton in a hydrogen bond at state $\ket{11}$ over time $t$ up to 40 fs. Refined compiled circuits at $n=4$ track the exact continuous Hamiltonian evolution with maximum deviation $\le 0.0042$.

fields.result: Complex Langevin search combined with Lefschetz-thimble Monte Carlo integration reproduces the high-temperature partition function and imaginary-time Green function $G(\tau)$ of the four-body SYK model. Path integral weight is heavily concentrated near the real axis, with the origin contributing about $2.3\%$ of the average real weight while complex saddle points fall to order $10^{-4}$.
fields.question: Can complex Langevin dynamics correctly locate all contributing saddle points and evaluate the Lefschetz-thimble path integral for the sign-problematic Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model?
fields.limits: Statistically equivalent representation of four-body SYK rather than identical Hamiltonian; tested up to $N = 32$ fermions and $N_\tau = 16$ time slices; importance sampling truncates at weight $e^{-18}$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Comparison of the imaginary-time Green function $\text{G}(\tau)$ evaluated across three frameworks fixed at $\beta=1$ , $N=16$ , and $N_{\tau}=16$ . Colored dashed lines represent the infrared-limit solutions, solid markers denote the continuous Monte Carlo integrations, and black crosses indicate the discrete DQMC after reweighting ( $10^{4}$ sampling sweeps). Both numerical schemes accurately enforce the algebraic constraint $\text{G}(0)=\text{G}(\beta)=0.5$ and display excellent agreement.
fields.figure_gloss: Imaginary-time Green function $G(\tau)$ plotted against $\tau$ at $\beta=1$, $N=16$, and $N_\tau=16$. Compares continuous Lefschetz-thimble Monte Carlo integration, sign-reweighted discrete DQMC, and infrared-limit theoretical curves across three values of coupling $J$.

fields.result: The universal lower bound $4\mathcal{F}_A \le \mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{NL}}_{\mathrm{lin}}$ holds across >260 nuclei and approaches saturation for weakly entangled states. Odd-odd nuclei exhibit distinct quantum complexity patterns compared to even-even and odd-even systems, showing elevated non-local magic alongside low entanglement spectrum antiflatness.
fields.question: How do non-local non-stabilizerness, entanglement entropy, and entanglement spectrum antiflatness scale across nuclear ground states under a proton-neutron bipartition?
fields.prior: Exact equality $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{NL}}_{\mathrm{lin}}=4\mathcal{F}_A$ held for two-qubit systems, and the bound was theoretically proven for general bipartitions without large-scale verification across physical nuclear states.
fields.limits: Calculations neglect isospin-breaking and electromagnetic interactions; non-local non-stabilizerness is approximated using an auxiliary Schmidt-decomposed state.
tools: Markov Chain Monte Carlo Pauli sampling
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Non-local non-stabilizerness $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{NL}}_{\mathrm{lin}}(\ket{\Psi})$ against $4\mathcal{F}_{A}$ for the ground states of $>260$ nuclei, with the proton-neutron bipartition. The purple dashed line is $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{NL}}_{\mathrm{lin}}=4\mathcal{F}_{A}$ . The green, red, and blue colors correspond to nuclei of the $p$ -, $sd$ - and $pf$ -shell, respectively. The shades distinguish nuclei with even and/or odd numbers of protons and neutrons. The vertical grey dashed line shows the maximal antiflatness for qubit systems [ 72 ] .
fields.figure_gloss: Non-local linear magic $\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{NL}}_{\mathrm{lin}}$ versus $4\mathcal{F}_A$ across >260 nuclei; all points lie above the equality line $4\mathcal{F}_A=\mathcal{M}^{\mathrm{NL}}_{\mathrm{lin}}$, with odd-odd nuclei showing distinct elevation above the bound.

fields.result: Establishes a quantitative hierarchy of rates enabling local AFM-tip driving of a suspended carbon nanotube coupled dispersively to a Cooper-pair box for phonon-parity mapping and quantum-capacitance readout. At $10$ mK, baseline thermal phonon occupations are $3.38$ for a $54$ MHz mode, $0.53$ for a $221$ MHz mode, and near the ground state for a $5.37$ GHz mode.
fields.question: How large can a resonant driving force applied by an atomic force microscope tip be before static softening, frequency fluctuations, dephasing, and heating overwhelm coherent control of a suspended carbon nanotube resonator?
fields.limits: Single-mode Duffing model neglecting higher flexural modes and internal resonances; rotating-wave approximation for weak Kerr anharmonicity; linearized resolved-sideband cooling model.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Thermal occupation and active cooling of representative CNT modes. ( a ) Thermal phonon occupation $\bar{n}_{\mathrm{th}}$ at $T=10$ mK as a function of CNT mechanical frequency. Red circles indicate the representative modes at $54$ MHz, $221$ MHz, and $5.37$ GHz. ( b ) Final phonon occupation $\bar{n}_{f}$ as a function of cooling cooperativity $\mathcal{C}$ for the $221$ MHz mode (blue continuous curve) and the $54$ MHz mode (dotted orange curve), using $\bar{n}_{f}\simeq\bar{n}_{\mathrm{th}}/(1+\mathcal{C})$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Thermal phonon occupation at $10$ mK across mechanical frequencies alongside final occupation after resolved-sideband cooling for $54$ MHz, $221$ MHz, and $5.37$ GHz modes.

fields.result: Symmetric bilayer WSeS with S/S stacking yields dominant trion emission at cryogenic temperatures and high thermal stability, driven by electron-phonon coupling strength of 3.9 resonant with optical phonon $A_1^2$ energy of 51 meV.
fields.question: Can tailoring interfacial architecture and built-in dipoles in Janus homobilayers achieve thermally robust trion emission via strong electron-phonon coupling?
fields.limits: Specific to symmetric S/S stacking configuration with inward-pointing antiparallel built-in electric fields.

fields.result: Emergent flux of a magnetic skyrmion transfers to an exciton as a full flux quantum $\pm\nu$ only when exchange coupling exceeds the spin-orbit threshold $J^*=|\Delta_{\mathrm{BD}}|/2$ (or $\Delta_c$), vanishing completely below it.
fields.question: How do composite neutral excitons with constituent-dependent spin-orbit coupling perceive and interact with topological magnetic spin textures?
fields.limits: Projected description holds in adiabatic regime ($J_i > \hbar^2/(2m_i w^2)$ and $J_i \neq \Delta_i$); two-dimensional semiconductor assumption; low temperature (4.2 K).
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Spin–orbit coupling switches the emergent flux. Skyrmion radius 10 nm, wall parameter 4 nm, $J_{v}=0.5$ meV, bright–dark splitting $\Delta_{\mathrm{BD}}=5$ meV, kinetic energy $k_{\mathrm{B}}T$ at 4.2 K; $K$ valley in blue, $K^{\prime}$ in orange. The shaded region, $J_{c}>J^{*}=\Delta_{\mathrm{BD}}/2$ , marks the dark core. a , Net emergent flux of the branch connected to the bright exciton versus $J_{c}/\Delta_{\mathrm{BD}}$ . b , Scattering skew and c , elastic cross-section from the exact two-channel solution (symbols) and from the gauge-field theory (dashed lines); the narrow gauge-field resonances in $K^{\prime}$ are clipped at 150 nm. d , Bright-to-dark leakage of the exact solution relative to elastic scattering, which signals the breakdown of adiabatic following. In $K^{\prime}$ , the dark channel is closed for $J_{c}/\Delta_{\mathrm{BD}}>0.54$ (dotted line), and there is no leakage.
fields.figure_gloss: Emergent flux $\Phi/\Phi_0$ and scattering properties as a function of the exchange-to-splitting ratio $J_c/\Delta_{\mathrm{BD}}$ for $K$ and $K'$ valleys, demonstrating the threshold switch to quantized flux and agreement with exact scattering calculations.

fields.result: Additional work deficit from total spin conservation in a charged Hubbard double quantum dot vanishes above a thermal crossover at $s_{2}=q$, occurring at $k_{B}T_{c}/t_{0} \simeq 0.11607$ for detuning-noise amplitude $\sigma_{\epsilon}/t_{0}=0.10$.
fields.question: How does spin conservation limit the extractable work of an interacting Hubbard double quantum dot charged in the presence of quasistatic detuning fluctuations?
fields.limits: Quasistatic Gaussian detuning disorder only (no $1/f$ time-resolved noise). Neglects higher orbitals, spin-orbit coupling, phonons, and finite pulse discharge protocols. Direct one-photon transition at representative parameters corresponds to $0.48\text{ THz}$ barrier modulation.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 6: Thermal crossover of the spin work deficit under detuning noise. (a) $\mathcal{G}_{\rm ST}/t_{0}=\bigl(\mathcal{W}_{U(1)}-\mathcal{W}_{N,S}\bigr)/t_{0}$ versus $k_{B}T/t_{0}$ and quasistatic detuning-noise amplitude $\sigma_{\epsilon}/t_{0}$ , at fixed $\tau=17$ . The solid boundary follows the numerically determined condition $s_{2}=q$ on the branch $q<s_{1}$ ; the full positive-part expression is used at all grid points. The red marker identifies the reference crossover at $\sigma_{\epsilon}/t_{0}=0.10$ , examined in panels (b) and (c). (b) Second singlet eigenvalue $s_{2}$ and population $q$ of each triplet as functions of temperature at $\sigma_{\epsilon}/t_{0}=0.10$ ; their crossing occurs at $k_{B}T_{c}/t_{0}\simeq 0.11607$ . (c) Corresponding constrained ergotropies of the same averaged state. Parameters: $U/t_{0}=14$ , $V/t_{0}=3$ , $A_{t}/t_{0}=0.10$ , $\omega_{d}=\Delta_{\rm eff}/\hbar$ ; $\mu=\mu_{12}^{(T)}$ is recalculated at each temperature. The boundary marks a change in passive spectral ordering, not a phase transition.
